name: OpenSSL
summary: A cryptographic and secure-protocol toolkit that separates protocol use, cryptographic operations, and provider-supplied algorithm implementations.

features.name: Protocol and cryptography library separation
features.description: OpenSSL provides libssl for TLS, DTLS, and QUIC protocol implementations and libcrypto as a general-purpose cryptographic library that can also be used independently.
benefits: Allows protocol implementations and independent cryptographic consumers to share primitives
Makes protocol and primitive APIs distinct integration boundaries
costs: Applications must understand more than one library boundary
Protocol behavior and cryptographic implementation selection can fail at different layers

features.name: Provider-supplied algorithm implementations
features.description: OpenSSL providers supply implementations for operations such as digests, ciphers, MACs, KDFs, key management, signatures, encoding, and decoding through dispatch and algorithm-query interfaces. Providers may be built in or dynamically loadable.
benefits: Permits multiple implementations of an algorithm behind stable library APIs
Supports default, FIPS, legacy, and third-party implementation domains
costs: Provider loading and compatibility become part of application configuration
Unqualified naming collisions can leave implementation selection unspecified

features.name: Property-directed algorithm fetching
features.description: An algorithm use can explicitly fetch an implementation from providers using a library context, algorithm identifier, and property query. OpenSSL also supports implicit fetching for compatibility APIs.
benefits: Makes implementation selection explicit when policy or provider identity matters
Allows one application to maintain separate library contexts
costs: Property queries and provider activation add configuration complexity
Implicit fetching can obscure which implementation is selected

features.name: Contextual cryptographic operation lifecycle
features.description: The documented libcrypto operation pattern creates an operation context, initializes it with an algorithm and parameters, accepts one or more updates, finalizes output, and releases the context and fetched objects.
benefits: Supports streaming input and operation-specific state
Provides a common lifecycle for digest, cipher, signature, and related operations
costs: Call ordering and resource cleanup are part of application correctness
Operation contexts do not by themselves specify protocol-level safety

mathematical_views.question: Which provider implementation is selected for an algorithm operation under a library context and property query?
assumptions: Providers expose finite named implementation sets for each operation
The library context determines the provider set considered by fetching
The view models selection and does not claim equivalence between implementations

mathematical_views.question: How does a streaming cryptographic operation move from allocation through initialization, updates, finalization, and cleanup?
assumptions: Operation contexts are modeled as stateful objects with ordered transitions
Initialization and finalization may reject invalid inputs
Provider-specific implementation details are abstracted behind the operation API

benefits: Reusable cryptographic primitives across protocol and non-protocol consumers
costs: Multiple APIs and failure boundaries must be integrated by applications
Provider lifecycle and selection policy increase operational surface
Queries, contexts, and fallback behavior complicate reasoning
State ordering and cleanup are required for correct use
